body:
## What

When the bulk scanner in `dump_escaped_impl()` stops at a control character, a quote or a backslash, that byte went through the UTF-8 decoder and a `switch` that wrote the escape byte by byte into `string_buffer`. The buffer was then copied into `write_buffer` at the next unescaped run.

A byte below 0x60 at a character boundary is a complete code point, so it now skips the decoder. Its escape sequence comes from a 96-entry table with 8-byte rows: the sequence is padded with zeros, and the last byte holds its length. All 8 bytes are copied straight into `write_buffer` after one room check, and the position advances by the length. The idea comes from orjson's `QUOTE_TAB`. Most of the gain comes from skipping the `string_buffer` round trip, not from the table. A table-only variant that still went through `string_buffer` gained only 2–7 %.

The check sits inside the existing character-boundary block, so it runs once each time the scanner stops, not once per byte. A first version tested every byte and cost about 6 % on twitter.json with `ensure_ascii`, where every byte of a CJK character went through the extra comparison.

The `switch` in the decoder's accept branch lost its cases for characters below 0x60, which can no longer reach it. What is left is "\u-escape under `ensure_ascii`, else copy the byte".

Changes:
- `detail/output/serializer.hpp`: the table (`ascii_escapes()`), the direct write in `dump_escaped_impl()`, and the smaller accept branch.
- `tests/src/unit-serialization.cpp`: new test case and updated string-buffer boundary tests (see below).

## Performance

Compact `dump()`, `dump(-1, ' ', true)` (ensure_ascii) and `dump(2)`, in ms: `develop` → this PR. Each cell is the median of 3 rounds × 101 runs. The first four rows are the usual corpus files. The last three rows are synthetic and escape-heavy:
- **json_in_json**: an array of 20 strings that each hold the compact dump of twitter.json (10 MB output, a quote every few bytes).
- **win_paths**: 100k strings like `C:\Users\name\AppData\Local\Temp\file123.txt`.
- **log_lines**: 100k strings like `line one\n\tline "two"\r\nend 123`.

**Apple clang 21, M1 Max (arm64)**

| document | compact | ensure_ascii | indent 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| canada | 7.17 → 7.22 (+1%) | 7.05 → 7.06 (+0%) | 8.19 → 8.28 (+1%) |
| citm | 0.58 → 0.58 (+1%) | 0.52 → 0.54 (+3%) | 0.81 → 0.81 (+0%) |
| twitter | 0.48 → 0.48 (-1%) | 0.56 → 0.57 (+2%) | 0.53 → 0.52 (-2%) |
| twitterescaped | 0.48 → 0.47 (-2%) | 0.56 → 0.57 (+2%) | 0.53 → 0.52 (-2%) |
| json_in_json | 14.41 → 11.92 (-17%) | 14.91 → 13.36 (-10%) | 13.84 → 11.26 (-19%) |
| win_paths | 9.62 → 8.24 (-14%) | 9.11 → 7.40 (-19%) | 9.56 → 7.91 (-17%) |
| log_lines | 7.61 → 5.88 (-23%) | 5.68 → 4.60 (-19%) | 7.61 → 5.82 (-24%) |

**GCC 13.3, x86-64 (VPS)**

| document | compact | ensure_ascii | indent 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| canada | 13.63 → 13.93 (+2%) | 13.31 → 13.63 (+2%) | 16.43 → 16.48 (+0%) |
| citm | 1.36 → 1.35 (-1%) | 1.27 → 1.30 (+2%) | 1.92 → 1.98 (+3%) |
| twitter | 1.02 → 1.02 (+0%) | 1.24 → 1.33 (+7%) | 1.15 → 1.14 (-1%) |
| twitterescaped | 1.02 → 1.02 (-0%) | 1.26 → 1.24 (-1%) | 1.13 → 1.12 (-1%) |
| json_in_json | 32.90 → 26.43 (-20%) | 38.69 → 32.35 (-16%) | 30.90 → 23.64 (-24%) |
| win_paths | 20.37 → 15.69 (-23%) | 20.91 → 16.82 (-20%) | 20.14 → 14.53 (-28%) |
| log_lines | 14.32 → 11.63 (-19%) | 12.52 → 9.91 (-21%) | 15.73 → 12.70 (-19%) |

**clang 18.1, x86-64 (VPS)**

| document | compact | ensure_ascii | indent 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| canada | 16.73 → 16.03 (-4%) | 16.63 → 16.23 (-2%) | 18.96 → 18.86 (-1%) |
| citm | 1.16 → 1.13 (-3%) | 1.07 → 1.07 (-0%) | 1.47 → 1.47 (+0%) |
| twitter | 1.06 → 1.04 (-1%) | 1.20 → 1.19 (-0%) | 1.13 → 1.11 (-2%) |
| twitterescaped | 1.00 → 1.05 (+5%) | 1.14 → 1.19 (+4%) | 1.09 → 1.12 (+3%) |
| json_in_json | 31.76 → 26.85 (-15%) | 32.23 → 30.64 (-5%) | 30.22 → 24.64 (-18%) |
| win_paths | 19.25 → 16.66 (-13%) | 16.98 → 15.39 (-9%) | 17.82 → 15.69 (-12%) |
| log_lines | 13.06 → 11.41 (-13%) | 10.36 → 9.11 (-12%) | 12.75 → 11.75 (-8%) |

Escape-heavy strings get 5–28 % faster on every compiler and in every mode. Documents with few escapes are unchanged within noise. The VPS has some background load: `twitter` and `twitterescaped` produce the same output, yet their rows there differ by up to 8 points, so differences of a few percent mean nothing on x86. On the M1, I repeated twitter and citm with `ensure_ascii` 5 × 401 times. The result was a small but steady cost of +1.4 % (twitter, 573 → 581 µs) and +1.5 % (citm, 516 → 524 µs): one extra comparison per non-ASCII character that is `\u`-escaped. Without `ensure_ascii`, both were 1 % faster.

I also measured part (b) of the same idea, writing without a bounds check per `put_char`/`put_literal`. A ceiling hack that removed those checks entirely, with one 16-byte room check per element instead, made no measurable difference on canada/citm/twitter. So that part is not in this PR.

## Tests

- New test case `characters below 0x60 are escaped from a table straight into the write buffer`:
  - every ASCII character (0x00–0x7F) at every position of strings of length 1–17, which crosses the scanner's 8-byte strides, compared against a separately written reference escaper with `ensure_ascii` off and on
  - runs of escaped characters
  - escapes straddling the end of the 1024-byte write buffer at every offset
  - pending `\u` escapes of non-ASCII characters in `string_buffer` that must be written before a table escape
  - escapes after invalid UTF-8 for all four error handlers
- The two `serialization boundary values for the string buffer` sections built their margins from runs of `\n`. Simple escapes no longer reach `string_buffer`, so they use U+00E4 under `ensure_ascii` (6-byte `\u00e4` steps; 83 characters leave the tightest 14-byte margin, and 84 trigger the flush) to keep covering the `< 13` guard.
- Differential check against `develop`, run locally and not committed, with identical output and exception messages in all 4,879,360 cases. Inputs: 400k random strings from a pool of control characters, `"`, `\`, 0x7F, letters, and valid and invalid UTF-8 lead and continuation bytes, plus every byte 0x00–0xFF at every position of lengths 1–40. Each one ran with `ensure_ascii` off and on × all four error handlers, also under ASan/UBSan with assertions enabled.
- The benchmark outputs (all 7 documents, all 3 modes) hash identically to `develop` on all three compilers.
- Full test suite with ASan/UBSan: 145/145 passed. The new test code is clean with clang's `-Weverything` (C++11 and C++20), with GCC 16's CI warning flags, and with clang-tidy.
- New test case `invalid UTF-8 at every position is handled like the reference` (commit c403f9319). It compares `dump()` with a second, separately written reference serializer, which decodes UTF-8 strictly (Unicode Table 3-7). It runs all four error handlers with `ensure_ascii` off and on, and for `strict` it checks the exception id and message. It covers:
  - 33 ill-formed patterns: stray continuation bytes, C0/C1/F5–FF, overlong encodings, surrogates, code points above U+10FFFF, and sequences cut short by ASCII, a control character, `"`, `\`, DEL, a lead byte, or the end of the string
  - every position of strings up to 40 bytes, filled with ASCII and with 2-, 3- and 4-byte characters
  - strings whose escaped form crosses the 512-byte `string_buffer`
  - repeated patterns at every offset of the end of that buffer

  It takes about 0.8 s in an unoptimized build and finds no differences. Each of these temporary mutations made it fail:
  - `< 13` → `< 1` in each of the three flush checks (accept, `replace`, `keep`)
  - removing the `--i` re-read in the `ignore`/`replace` branch, and in the `keep` branch
  - missing the last byte of an 8-byte word in `find_string_special` or `find_ascii_copyable_run`

  The flush-check mutations are caught by the assertion in `write_u_escape`, so only in builds with assertions enabled.

The new test passes on `develop` too, so it also serves as a regression test for the escaper as it is now.

## Breaking changes

None. Only the way escapes are written changed. The output is byte-identical, and all changes are in `detail`.

review_comments.diff_hunk:
@@ -1253,6 +1227,121 @@ class serializer
         }
     }
 
+    /*!
+    @brief the JSON form of each character below 0x60
+
+    Entry c holds the escape sequence of character c - the short form for
+    \\b, \\t, \\n, \\f, \\r, \\" and \\\\, \\u00xx for the other control characters -
+    or c itself if it needs no escaping, padded with zeros to 7 bytes. The last
+    byte is the length of the sequence. The 8 bytes of an entry are copied at
+    once, so writing an escape needs neither a branch nor a byte-wise loop.

review_comments.body:
The `memcpy` deliberately copies all 8 bytes: with a constant size it compiles to one 64-bit load/store, whereas a variable-size copy becomes a call or a branch cascade. So the room check has to cover 8 bytes, not `escape[7]` — checking only `escape[7]` while copying 8 could write past the end of `write_buffer`. One could add 7 bytes of slack to the buffer and check the real length, but that only saves an occasional flush a few bytes early once per 1 KiB, which doesn't change the output and isn't measurable. I'd keep it as is.

*(Written by Claude Code.)*

Then the sequence starts at offset 1, and an 8-byte copy from `data() + 1` would read into the next entry (and past the array for 0x5F). The options are a 7-byte copy (two stores instead of one) or 9-byte entries (losing alignment). The trailing zeros are only how the table looks in the source and cost nothing at runtime, so I'd rather keep the single aligned store.

*(Written by Claude Code.)*
